[[File:Great dodecahemicosahedron.stl|thumb|3D model of a great dodecahemicosahedron]]
In [[geometry]], the '''great dodecahemicosahedron''' (or '''small dodecahemiicosahedron'''<!-- NOT A TYPO, JOHNSON 2000 SWAPS THE NAMES -->) is a [[nonconvex uniform polyhedron]], indexed as U<sub>65</sub>. It has 22 faces (12 [[Pentagon|pentagons]] and 10 [[Hexagon|hexagons]]), 60 edges, and 30 vertices.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mathconsult.ch/static/unipoly/65.html|title=65: great dodecahemicosahedron|last=Maeder|first=Roman|website=MathConsult}}</ref> Its [[vertex figure]] is a [[quadrilateral#More quadrilaterals|crossed quadrilateral]].

It is a [[hemipolyhedron]] with ten hexagonal faces passing through the model center.

== Related polyhedra ==

Its [[convex hull]] is the [[icosidodecahedron]]. It also shares its [[edge arrangement]] with the [[dodecadodecahedron]] (having the pentagonal faces in common), and with the [[small dodecahemicosahedron]] (having the hexagonal faces in common).

=== Great dodecahemicosacron ===
{{Uniform polyhedra db|Uniform dual polyhedron stat table|gDhI|No-Face-Image=True}}
The '''great dodecahemicosacron''' is the dual of the great dodecahemicosahedron, and is one of nine [[dual hemipolyhedra]]. It appears visually indistinct from the [[small dodecahemicosacron]].

Since the hemipolyhedra have [[Face (geometry)|faces]] passing through the center, the [[Dual polyhedron|dual figures]] have corresponding [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] at infinity; properly, on the [[real projective plane]] at infinity.<ref>{{Harv|Wenninger|2003|loc = [https://books.google.com/books?id=mfmzUjhs-_8C&pg=PA101 p. 101]}}</ref> In [[Magnus Wenninger]]'s ''Dual Models'', they are represented with intersecting [[prism (geometry)|prisms]], each extending in both directions to the same vertex at infinity, in order to maintain symmetry. In practice, the model prisms are cut off at a certain point that is convenient for the maker. Wenninger suggested these figures are members of a new class of [[stellation]] figures, called ''stellation to infinity''. However, he also suggested that strictly speaking, they are not polyhedra because their construction does not conform to the usual definitions.

The great dodecahemicosahedron can be seen as having ten [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] at infinity.
